asDecan.p: Astrologers cut each sign into three ten-degree slices called decans, and each slice gets a planet of its own and a small card to go with it. Your Sun sits somewhere between 10 and 19 degrees of Taurus, the middle slice, where the sign has settled in and is at its fullest. Venus runs Taurus as a whole, so underneath it's fixed earth, with a taste for good things and a strong dislike of being hurried. The Moon rules your ten degrees, and the Moon is exalted in Taurus. That's the old term for a planet treated as a guest of honour in a sign, the place where it shows its most idealised side. So you get the Moon's instinct to feed and look after people, in a sign that wants things solid enough to hold. The Five of Pentacles before you is Mercury's slice, and it frets about going without. The Seven after you belongs to Saturn and waits on a slow harvest. Yours is the one handing the coins out.

You notice what people need before they've said it, and you tend to answer with something they can actually hold. A friend mentions a rough week in a text and by Thursday there's a lasagne on their doorstep. At a family dinner you're the one watching whose glass is empty and who hasn't had seconds, and to be honest you'd prefer that job to sitting down. You keep a running list in your head of who likes what, the colleague who takes their tea weak, the nephew who won't touch anything green. Money matters to you mostly as a cushion, and you feel it in your stomach when the savings dip. A Sunday with nothing planned is close to perfect as long as the fridge is full and somebody drops round. You like being the house people come to.

The less obvious gift is in the scales the man is holding in the picture. You have a good feel for what's fair, and you can talk about money without anyone going red, which is rarer than it sounds. When a group holiday gets booked and one friend earns half what the others do, you're the one who quietly suggests splitting the house by room size. When a parent's estate has to be sorted, the siblings often want you there, because you'll say what each person needs and nobody feels judged for needing it. The exalted Moon gives you tact about need. You can usually tell whether someone wants the cash, the advice or just a hot meal, and you give them the right one. Friends who've borrowed from you tend to pay it back without being chased.

This one is harder to spot, because it looks like kindness. Giving is the comfortable seat on this card, and being on the receiving end makes you uneasy in a way you don't often admit. Your partner offers to cover the rent for a few months while you retrain, and you say yes and then spend the whole stretch slightly on edge, doing extra housework to square it. A friend pays for lunch and you've booked the next one before the plates are cleared. There's a power question under all this. The person holding the scales decides what counts as fair, and part of you likes having that job. It can come out in an argument as well, a list of everything you've done for someone, brought out at the worst moment. People close to you sometimes feel they can never quite get level with you, so they keep a little distance.

Under strain you feed people. A death in the family, a friend's marriage ending, a bad round of layoffs at work, and your first move is the kitchen, the casserole dishes, the spare room made up. That's genuinely useful and people remember it for years. You also tighten up about money, sometimes quite hard, checking the account twice a day, cancelling small things, going quiet about spending with your partner. About a week later the caretaking has usually turned into a tiredness you haven't mentioned to anyone, and you start to get short with the people you've been looking after. That confuses them, since nobody asked for the third lasagne. What helps is letting one person look after you properly for an evening, a meal cooked for you, someone else doing the ringing round. Say yes to it and don't offer anything back.

You tend to fall for people you can look after, and it's worth knowing that about yourself. The one who's between jobs, a bit lost or recently heartbroken gets your attention faster than someone with everything sorted. That can work beautifully for a while. The risk is a relationship that sets into giver and receiver, until after a few years one of you feels like the benefactor and the other feels like a charity case, even if nobody says so. The ones that last usually have a partner in them who insists on looking after you back and won't take no for an answer. Physically the Moon here makes you affectionate in a slow, steady way. You need touch that isn't rushed, a hand on your back while you're cooking, a long lie-in on a Saturday, and you go a bit cold when it's missing.

The Hierophant is your Sun card, and it gives you the pull toward institutions and toward passing on what works. This decan narrows that down to resources, who gets what and whether it's fair. You're good anywhere money or care has to be shared out, payroll, grants, a hospital ward, a charity, running the budget for a small team. People trust you with the kitty. You're often the one who notices the junior being underpaid or the client being overcharged, and you raise it, politely, more than once. Hospitality suits you as well, since feeding strangers properly is a very Moon in Taurus thing to be paid for. The usual trap is taking on other people's workload because you can see they're struggling. Help one person well and let the others ask.

At twenty this slice of Taurus often plays host before it can really afford to. Yours is the flat everybody ends up in, feeding six people on a student budget and lending money you then lie awake about. You can be hurt when the favours go unnoticed. By the mid-thirties a lot of people with the Sun here have something under them, a house or a steady job or some savings, and the giving gets calmer and better judged. It's common around then to work out which friends return things and which just take, and to let a couple of friendships go quietly. The fifties are often generous years for this decan in both directions. There's more to give, and many people with this placement finally get easier about being given to, by grown children, by old friends, sometimes by a partner who's waited a long time to do it.

Once a week, accept something without evening it up. A coffee someone buys you, a lift home, a colleague covering your shift. Say thank you and leave it there. Don't send a gift the next day, don't offer to get the next one, and don't do an extra job around the house to square it. Keep a note on your phone of what you were given and how long the urge to repay it lasted. Most people with this decan find the urge gets shorter after a month or so.
